content_units: Mortgage Offer Comparison at a Glance
Here’s the plain-language way to compare these offers: separate the decision into   monthly cost   and   upfront cost  , then ask how long you expect to keep the loan.
Offer   Rate   Points Cost   Lender Fees   Total Upfront Loan Costs   Est. Monthly Principal + Interest   Best Compared To
C   6.15%   $7,140   $6,400     $13,540       $2,176/mo     Lowest payment, highest upfront cost
These monthly payments are estimates for   principal and interest only  . They do   not   include taxes, insurance, HOA dues, or mortgage insurance.
Lower rate usually means lower monthly payment.
-   Offer C   has the   lowest payment  : about   $2,176/mo

Break-even means:   how many months it takes for monthly savings to repay the extra upfront cost  .
Break-even months = Extra upfront cost ÷ Monthly savings
Which Borrower Each Offer Fits Best
Option 1:   Offer B — Lowest upfront cash need     Best if you want to keep closing costs low and may not keep the mortgage very long     Cheapest to start
Option 2:   Offer A — Balanced middle choice     Good if you want some payment reduction without paying as much upfront as Offer C     Moderate payment, moderate fees
Option 3:   Offer C — Best for long-term holders     Makes more sense if you expect to keep the loan well past the break-even point     Lowest monthly payment
- Choose   Offer B   if cash at closing matters most or you may refinance/sell within roughly   10 years  .
- Choose   Offer A   if you want a   compromise   between monthly savings and upfront cost.
- Choose   Offer C   if you are very likely to keep the mortgage   longer than about 10 years   and can comfortably afford the extra upfront cash.
-   Shorter stay in the loan:   usually favor   fewer points / lower upfront cost
-   Longer stay in the loan:   paying points can make sense
To keep the comparison clean, this assumes:
- Only   points + lender fees   are compared upfront
- Other closing costs are similar across all 3 offers
- Monthly payment shown is only   principal + interest
